stem: During external-beam radiation therapy, a client develops an area in the treatment field where the skin is peeling, moist, and painful. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: Notify the radiation care team, assess the affected skin, keep the area clean and dry as directed, and use only the dressings or skin products recommended for the treatment field.
options.B: Clean the area vigorously with soap and a washcloth to remove peeling tissue, then leave it uncovered so moisture does not remain against the irradiated skin.
options.C: Apply an adhesive bandage and an over-the-counter antibiotic ointment to protect the moist area, then report it only if the drainage or pain becomes worse.
options.D: Keep the area dry and avoid friction, but delay reporting the change because moist peeling is an expected radiation effect that usually resolves after therapy ends.

rationale: NCI describes a moist reaction as irradiated skin that peels and becomes moist and painful; sores or ulcers can develop and may lead to infection. NCI advises clients to report skin changes so they can be treated promptly and recommends keeping a peeling, painful, wet radiation area clean and dry using the care plan provided by the radiation team. The team may prescribe special dressings or antibiotics when indicated, and NCI advises against unapproved bandages or skin products in the treatment area. Therefore A is correct. B adds traumatic scrubbing, C uses an unapproved adhesive and self-selected topical treatment while delaying reporting, and D delays reporting a skin complication that warrants directed supportive care.
educational_objective: Recognize moist radiation skin reaction as painful wet desquamation that requires prompt reporting and radiation-team-directed gentle skin care, including clean/dry management and only recommended dressings or products.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health

source_claim_supported: Moist radiation reaction is painful wet peeling skin with infection risk; skin changes should be reported promptly, the area should be kept clean and dry using team-directed care, and only recommended dressings/products should be used in the treatment field.

correction_summary: Rebuilt all four actions to remove the uniquely-long keyed answer and replace simplistic distractors with realistic errors involving traumatic cleansing, unapproved adhesive/topical treatment, and delayed reporting. The corrected item uses current NCI guidance with direct locators for moist reaction, clean/dry care, recommended products, and radiation-field bandage avoidance.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Radiation therapy adverse effect — moist skin reaction/desquamation
audit_findings.stem: PASS — the moist, painful peeling treatment-field skin matches the NCI definition of a moist reaction and asks one immediate nursing-care decision.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — combines prompt team notification, assessment, clean/dry supportive care, and use of recommended treatment-field products; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — cleansing is relevant, but vigorous rubbing of already damaged irradiated skin adds avoidable trauma.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — wound protection may be needed, but NCI advises against unapproved adhesive bandages and directs use of team-recommended products rather than self-selected topical therapy.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — dry protection and friction avoidance may be helpful, but delaying reporting conflicts with NCI guidance to report skin changes promptly for treatment.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only option that follows the full source-supported response without adding trauma, unapproved products, or delayed evaluation.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B uses traumatic cleansing, C introduces unapproved treatment and delay, and D postpones reporting of a recognized complication.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — all four options are closely matched in length and specificity and the keyed answer is not uniquely long.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Basic Care and Comfort directly includes skin/tissue integrity measures, comfort interventions, and pain assessment.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether keeping the area dry without immediate reporting or applying a protective adhesive could be defensible; NCI specifically calls for prompt reporting, team-directed clean/dry care, recommended products, and avoidance of adhesive bandages in the field, leaving A uniquely best.
